title: architecture-review-kv-cache-splitter-sla-discussion-2026-07-13
content:
Architecture review notes: KV cache splitter - SLA/latency and fallback discussion (2026-07-13)

Attendees:
- Alex Chen (owner, notes)
- Priya Kapoor
- Diego Morales
- Hannah Li
- Samir Patel
- Guest: Jordan R. (SRE)

Agenda:
1) Quick recap of splitter design goals and constraints
2) Impact of splitter on P99 tail latency and regional SLAs
3) Fallback behavior when splitter misroutes or a shard is overloaded
4) Consistency and retention implications (eviction + replication)
5) Action items and next steps

Recap:
- Splitter is intended to route KV cache requests across multiple cache partitions to improve throughput and reduce hot shards. Current prototype implements hash-based partitioning with optional short-circuiting for small sessions. See RFC-142 and follow-ups.
- Major concerns raised in prior meetings: (a) P99 tail due to cross-shard coordination, (b) correctness on migration/reshard, (c) operational complexity for multi-tenant workloads.

Discussion highlights:
1) P99 tail and SLA impact:
- Jordan: Observed that adding a remote lookup to a second shard increases P99 by ~8-12ms in our internal microbenchmarks for 8K token contexts; worst-case when KV miss causes a synchronous fetch to remote partition.
- Priya: For Hosted customers with 99th percentile SLO of 200ms, an extra 10-15ms is acceptable if it's bounded and predictable; the problem is unbounded variability when network retries or GC pauses occur.
- Diego: Proposed async-prefetch path for likely-miss keys (ML-based predictor) so that misses don't block the main token generation path. Concern: prefetch increases background load and could amplify cascade failures under burst.
- Decision (tentative): Implement bounded-sync lookup with strict per-request timeout (5ms) plus an async-prefetch pipeline. If bounded lookup times out, use a local fallback and annotate trace for quality monitoring.

2) Fallback behavior and graceful degradation:
- Hannah: We need deterministic fallback rules to preserve safety and observability. Options discussed:
  a) Local in-memory fallback (fast, lower hit quality)
  b) Fallback to smaller model variant that doesn't rely on KV cache (costly)
  c) Recompute prefix on the fly (expensive and increases latency)
- Samir: Recommended default to local in-memory fallback + mark responses with a special header/trace tag so downstream services can decide to retry or accept lower-quality output.
- Decision: Default fallback will be local in-memory short-lived cache. For enterprise customers that require higher consistency, allow a per-tenant policy to prefer cross-shard guarantees with an increased latency SLO and observability flags.

3) Consistency, resharding, and retention:
- Diego: Raised concerns about stale entries during migration. Two approaches: synchronous migration (copy-and-swap) vs lazy rehashing (move-on-access).
- Priya: Copy-and-swap provides stronger consistency at higher cost during reshard windows; lazy rehashing is lower-cost but requires stronger TTL+vector clocks to avoid stale reads.
- Decision: Use copy-and-swap for Dedicated and Private deployments where we control maintenance windows. For Hosted, use lazy rehashing with versioned keys + short grace TTLs and background reconciliation jobs. Add telemetry to surface reshard-related misses.

4) Operational guardrails and tooling:
- Jordan: We must have automated circuit breakers for splitter-induced load amplification (rate limit prefetches per shard, backpressure on request ingress).
- Hannah: Add per-tenant cost/latency budget and auto-fallback policy. If a tenant exceeds budget, lower prefetch aggressiveness and switch to local fallback.
- Action: Build an ops dashboard showing shard hotness, prefetch hit/miss ratios, P99 delta vs baseline, and tenant-level cost impact.

5) Security and multi-tenant isolation:
- Samir: Confirmed KV cache entries include tenant-scoped keys. Any cross-shard routing must preserve tenant boundaries and never mix tenant contexts.
- Decision: Enforce tenant-prefixing at the splitter layer and add a test suite that fuzzes cross-tenant routing.

Open questions / risks:
- ML predictor false positives: risk of over-prefetching under adversarial or bursty workloads. Need simulated load tests.
- Latency variance from cloud network: upper bound timeouts may need to differ by region.
- Cost/benefit for enterprise tenants: whether to provide a paid option for synchronous cross-shard consistency.

Action items (owners & ETA):
- Priya: Prototype async prefetch pipeline + rate limiter (ETA: 2026-07-27) [linked to GitHub PR].
- Diego: Implement bounded-sync lookup with 5ms timeout and local fallback in prototype (ETA: 2026-07-20).
- Hannah: Design dashboard wireframes for shard hotness and prefetch telemetry (ETA: 2026-07-24).
- Jordan (SRE): Add circuit-breaker prototype and run chaos tests for prefetch amplification (ETA: 2026-08-03).
- Samir: Draft tenant policy options and add integration tests for tenant isolation (ETA: 2026-07-30).

References & context:
- RFC-142: KV cache sharding (see earlier doc and comments)
- Previous notes: architecture-review-kv-cache-splitter-performance-tradeoffs-2026-07-06.json
- Linked artifacts: CONFLUENCE-8421 (design notes), SERV-3692 (ticket for prefetch work), PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/271

Next meeting:
- Tentatively 2026-07-27 for a prototype demo and early perf numbers.

Notes and tone:
- This doc is a working artifact: expect edits and clarifications. The decisions above are "tentative" until prototype telemetry confirms expected behavior.

End of notes.
